newsitem.title: UK: Sterling/mark off highs on profit-taking, Welteke.
newsitem.headline: Sterling/mark off highs on profit-taking, Welteke.

text.p: Sterling rode on the coattails of a charged dollar on Wednesday as both currencies surged to fresh highs before profit-taking and comments by a Bundesbank official pushed them firmly back, traders said.
Welteke said the mark could not continue to depreciate against the dollar at the pace seen over the last few days.
The dollar slipped after his comments, but found a solid base as buyers emerged on the dips, said Graham Cocks, senior dealer at Bank of Boston in London.
Weaker-than-expected December retail sales figures did not damper the pound's run, although analysts said the data could diminish prospects for an early February rate rise.
"They should provide (Chancellor of the Exchequer) Clarke with sufficient ammunition to hold off raising rates," said Paul Lambert, senior currency economist at UBS.
UK December retail sales dropped 0.8 percent on the month and rose 2.9 percent year-on-year, well below consensus forecasts of no change and a 3.5 increase respectively.

Sterling broke through key resistance at 2.1780 and hit a fresh 52-month high of 2.7240 marks in the session. It then settled back to 2.7133/43 marks at 1550 GMT, still up over a pfennig from its 2.7028/38 level in late Europe on Tuesday.
The 2.1780 level is a 61.8 percent Fibonacci retracement of the entire move from 3.0575 marks in October 1990 to the record low at 2.1683 in November 1995, chartists said.
The dollar's climb pushed cable lower to $1.6549/54, down from Tuesday's $1.6635/40 in late Europe.

Sterling should continue to receive support from the dollar's strength even as the market reasseses the likelihood of a rate rise at the February 5 monetary meeting between Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George, analysts said.
"One suspects the market's confidence that rates are going up before the election must increasingly be called into question," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi.
The next major UK data is fourth quarter GDP expected on Monday.
